screens.title: Securing Your VPC and Network Perimeter
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of an AWS Virtual Private Cloud and the controls that keep its perimeter and internal segments secure. We will treat the VPC like a virtual data center: there are instance-level firewalls called Security Groups, subnet-level filters called Network Access Control Lists, routing choices that determine which resources see the internet, and VPC Endpoints that let services talk privately inside the AWS backbone. You will see concrete examples such as allowing SSH only from a trusted IP range, how NACL rules are ordered and stateless, and how a Gateway Endpoint lets a private EC2 instance call S3 without an internet path. I will also point out common mistakes, like opening port 22 to the world or misordering NACL deny rules, and explain why auditing and DNS configuration matter as ongoing tasks. By the end of this chapter you will understand the relationships between these controls and be able to choose the right pattern to isolate sensitive resources while allowing necessary service access. Keep in mind: security in a VPC is layered and continuous, not a one-time checkbox.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Securing Your VPC
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Securing Your VPC and Network Perimeter

Build a layered security posture using Security Groups, NACLs, routing, and VPC Endpoints. Learn practical patterns and common mistakes to avoid.

In this lesson
Visual Preview
Layered cards show how traffic moves from Internet Gateway to subnets, through NACLs and Security Groups, and then to private service endpoints.
Why this matters

Misconfigurations at the network boundary can expose data or permit lateral movement. Layering controls reduces risk and makes audits easier.

Quick example
Use a Gateway Endpoint so an instance in a private subnet lists S3 without touching the public internet.
Explore Key Topics
Security Groups
Instance-level, stateful firewall for permitting required ports.
NACLs
Subnet-level, stateless filters processed by rule order.
VPC Endpoints
Private access to AWS services without crossing the public internet.
Network Snapshot
Internet Gateway
Routes public traffic to the internet
Private Subnet
No direct internet route; use NAT or Endpoints
VPC Endpoint
Private path for S3 or other services
Common pitfalls
  • Opening management ports to 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Adding DENY NACL rules without testing order and return paths.
  • Relying on default routing to keep resources private.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use to secure a VPC. First, you will be able to identify and describe core VPC components and how they interrelate, so you can reason about where to place protection. Second, you will learn to configure Security Groups correctly for least-privilege access, including concrete examples like permitting SSH only from a trusted management IP. Third, you will gain the ability to design and apply Network ACLs at the subnet level, and understand how stateless rules require explicit return port allowances. Fourth, you will learn how to choose and configure VPC Endpoints so service traffic stays on the AWS network and avoids the public internet. Each objective includes a competency milestone you can verify: describe the control, configure a minimal rule set, and validate behavior with a simple connection test.

screens.title: What is a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Virtual Private Cloud, or VPC, is a logically isolated portion of the AWS network where you create subnets, route tables, and gateways to control traffic. Think of it as your cloud data center. You define IP ranges with CIDR blocks and decide which subnets are public or private based on where you place an Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, or VPC Endpoints. A concrete example: you might create a VPC with two subnets — a public subnet for a load balancer attached to an Internet Gateway and a private subnet for application servers that never receive incoming internet traffic. That private subnet can still reach S3 privately through a Gateway Endpoint, avoiding the internet entirely. A common misconception is that resources inside a VPC are automatically private; in fact, a subnet becomes public when its route table directs 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway. So you must design subnets and routes deliberately. Key takeaway: the VPC is the foundation for all subsequent network controls. When you design one, draw expected traffic paths and explicitly map which control (Security Group, NACL, route table, endpoint) enforces each boundary.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a VPC?
Definition

Virtual Private Cloud

A logically isolated network in AWS where you control IP ranges, subnets, and routing.

Analogy
Treat the VPC like your private rack space in a cloud data center — you decide who can cross the perimeter.
Concrete example
Public subnet hosts a load balancer routed through an Internet Gateway; private subnet hosts databases with no default route to the Internet Gateway.
Common misconception
Resources in a VPC are not automatically private. A route to an Internet Gateway makes a subnet public.
Key Takeaway

Design subnets and routes deliberately: decide which workloads should be reachable from the internet and which should use private endpoints or NAT for outbound needs.

Topology Example
Public Subnet
Internet Gateway attached; used for load balancers.
Private Subnet
No IGW route; outbound via NAT or VPC Endpoint.
Gateway Endpoint
Routes S3 traffic privately via route table target.
Try this
Sketch your VPC CIDR and label which subnet needs an IGW, which needs a NAT, and where an endpoint would reduce internet exposure.

screens.title: Security Groups — instance-level, stateful controls
screens.narratorSegment: Security Groups are the primary instance-level firewall in AWS. They are stateful, which means once you permit an outbound request, the return traffic is implicitly allowed even if there is no explicit inbound rule for that return path. You attach one or more Security Groups to an EC2 instance or other supported resource and define only what is allowed; everything else is implicitly denied. A practical example: to allow SSH administration, add an inbound rule for TCP port 22 from your management IP range only. Avoid the common mistake of opening port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0, which exposes your hosts to the world. Security Groups support referencing other security groups as sources, which is a powerful pattern for allowing traffic from a specific application tier without relying on IPs. Misconception check: because Security Groups are permissive-only, you cannot explicitly deny traffic at the Security Group level. If you need explicit deny semantics, that is where NACLs can complement Security Groups at the subnet boundary. Key takeaway: design Security Groups for least privilege, reuse group references for tiers, and keep administration ports limited to known addresses.

keyIdea.title: Security Group rule model
keyIdea.text: Instance-level, stateful, permissive-only — specify allowances; rely on implicit deny for everything else.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Security Groups
Core Concept

Security Groups are stateful

They control traffic at the instance level and only define what is allowed; replies are automatically permitted.

Concrete example
Inbound TCP 22 from 198.51.100.5/32 to allow SSH from a management host.
Best practice
Reference other security groups for tier-to-tier traffic rather than opening broad IP ranges.
Common mistake
Using 0.0.0.0/0 for management ports like SSH or RDP; this invites wide scanning and brute force attempts.
Key Takeaway

Make Security Groups narrow and role-based; use group references to restrict inter-tier traffic without moving IPs.

Rule examples
# Example Security Group rules (conceptual)
Inbound:
- Allow TCP 22 from 198.51.100.5/32
- Allow TCP 443 from sg-app-tier
Outbound:
- Allow All traffic to 0.0.0.0/0  # replies and outbound requests
Notice the intent: inbound rules limit who can initiate connections. Outbound is often broader but should follow least-privilege when possible.
Check your understanding
If you allow outbound HTTPS to 0.0.0.0/0, do you need to add an inbound rule for the response? No — Security Groups are stateful and permit return traffic automatically.

screens.title: Network ACLs (NACLs) — subnet-level, stateless filters
screens.narratorSegment: Network Access Control Lists operate at the subnet boundary and are stateless. That means every direction of traffic must be explicitly allowed: if you allow inbound TCP 80, you must also allow outbound ephemeral ports such as 1024–65535 to permit return traffic. NACLs support both ALLOW and DENY rules and rules are evaluated in order by rule number from lowest to highest. When a packet matches a rule, that rule immediately applies and no further rules are processed. This ordered processing is a critical operational detail. A common use case is to place a NACL on a private subnet to block known malicious IP ranges before traffic reaches instances. But be cautious: adding DENY rules can inadvertently block legitimate traffic if rule numbers or ranges are not precise. Always test NACL changes in non-production or during a maintenance window. Concrete example: a NACL with a low-numbered DENY for a malicious IP will stop that IP at the subnet edge even if an instance Security Group would otherwise allow it. Key takeaway: NACLs are powerful gatekeepers but require careful ordering and explicit return rules because they are stateless.

keyIdea.text: NACLs are stateless subnet filters evaluated by rule order, and they can explicitly DENY traffic — use them carefully for subnet-wide protections.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Network ACLs (NACLs)
Core Concept

NACLs are stateless and ordered

They are evaluated by rule number; a match stops further processing. Both directions require explicit rules.

Concrete example
Allow inbound TCP 80 from 10.0.1.0/24 and allow outbound ephemeral 1024-65535 to 10.0.1.0/24 so return traffic flows.
Operational caution
A DENY rule with a low number can block all traffic unexpectedly. Always stage and test NACL changes.
Key Takeaway

Use NACLs for subnet-wide protections and explicit denies, but carefully manage rule order and return port allowances because NACLs are stateless.

NACL Rule Set Example
Inbound Rules (by number):
100 ALLOW TCP 80  from 10.0.1.0/24
110 ALLOW TCP 443 from 10.0.1.0/24
120 ALLOW TCP 22  from 10.0.1.0/24
130 ALLOW ALL     from 10.0.2.0/24
140 ALLOW TCP 1024-65535 from 10.0.1.0/24

Outbound Rules:
100 ALLOW ALL     to 10.0.1.0/24
110 ALLOW TCP 80  to 10.0.1.0/24
120 ALLOW TCP 443 to 10.0.1.0/24
130 ALLOW TCP 1024-65535 to 10.0.1.0/24
140 ALLOW TCP 443 to pl-63a5400a  # S3 prefix list (conceptual)
Remember: because this is stateless, both inbound and outbound directions must explicitly allow expected traffic ranges.

screens.title: Security Groups vs NACLs
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between Security Groups and NACLs is crucial for proper VPC design. Security Groups are stateful and apply to instances; they are permissive-only and ideal for defining which ports or sources an application tier accepts. NACLs are stateless, apply to subnets, and can include explicit deny rules. A practical contrast: if you want to prevent all traffic from a known malicious IP to an entire subnet, a low-numbered DENY in a NACL will stop that traffic before it reaches instances. Conversely, to restrict SSH to a particular management host for a single server, a Security Group rule referencing the management host's IP is cleaner and easier to manage. Another important operational note is order: NACLs process rules by number and stop at a match; Security Groups evaluate all rules together. Misconception: Security Groups cannot block traffic explicitly; they only allow. Use them for least-privilege access and use NACLs sparingly for broader deny patterns. The key takeaway: combine both controls — Security Groups for per-resource permissions, NACLs for subnet-level policies — and test changes because their behaviors differ in statefulness and rule processing.

keyIdea.text: Security Groups are for instance-level, stateful allowances; NACLs are for subnet-level, ordered, stateless filtering and explicit denies.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Security Groups vs NACLs
Security Groups

Stateful, instance-level

  • Define allowed inbound and outbound traffic; implicit deny otherwise.
  • Return traffic is allowed automatically because they are stateful.
  • Cannot explicitly deny traffic.
Use case
Restrict SSH, HTTPS, or inter-tier traffic to specific sources or security groups.
Network ACLs

Stateless, subnet-level

  • Process rules by number; stop at the first match.
  • Support explicit ALLOW and DENY rules.
  • Both inbound and outbound must be allowed for a connection to succeed.
Use case
Block malicious IP ranges at the subnet edge or enforce subnet-wide policies.
Quick decision guide
If you need per-instance control
Use Security Groups
If you need explicit denies
Use NACLs at the subnet boundary
Always remember
Combine both for layered security

screens.title: VPC Endpoints: Gateway and Interface
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Endpoints let resources talk to supported AWS services privately over the AWS network. There are two primary types you need to know: Gateway Endpoints and Interface Endpoints. Gateway Endpoints apply to S3 and DynamoDB. They are configured as a target in a route table and are free to use. An example: add a Gateway Endpoint for S3 to the private subnet's route table; EC2 instances can then upload to S3 without a NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway. Interface Endpoints use AWS PrivateLink and create an elastic network interface with a private IP in your subnet. They support many services and partner endpoints, but they incur charges. Use Interface Endpoints when Gateway Endpoints are not supported or when you need finer-grained control. A practical design: prefer Gateway Endpoints for S3 traffic to avoid NAT costs and reduce attack surface; use Interface Endpoints when you need private access to other AWS services. Misconception: endpoints always eliminate the need for secure policies — you still must use IAM and bucket policies to enforce access control. Key takeaway: choose the endpoint type by service and cost trade-off and associate endpoints with the correct route tables or subnets.

keyIdea.title: Endpoint selection
keyIdea.text: Gateway Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB (free); Interface Endpoints for other services (PrivateLink, paid). Associate them with the correct route tables and subnets.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › VPC Endpoints
Types

Gateway vs Interface

Gateway Endpoint
Used for S3 and DynamoDB; add as a route table target; no data plane charges for the endpoint itself.
Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink)
Creates an ENI in your subnet for private IP access to supported services; may incur charges.
Example
A private EC2 instance uploads logs to S3 via a Gateway Endpoint without touching the public internet.
Decision factors
  • Supported service: Gateway only for S3/DynamoDB.
  • Cost: Gateway endpoints are free; Interface endpoints may have hourly and data costs.
  • Network design: Interface endpoints create ENIs and can be placed in private subnets.
Key Takeaway

Use Gateway Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB to reduce internet exposure and NAT cost; use Interface Endpoints for other services when private connectivity is required.

screens.title: Subnetting and Routing Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A secure subnetting and routing strategy separates internet-facing components from private resources. Start by defining CIDR blocks and dividing them into public and private subnets. Public subnets should have a route to an Internet Gateway for workloads that need inbound access, like public load balancers. Private subnets should not have a default route to an Internet Gateway. Instead, private subnets often send outbound traffic through a NAT Gateway when instances need to reach the internet for updates, or through VPC Endpoints to reach AWS services privately. A typical design: place bastion hosts in a public subnet that only accepts SSH from an operations IP, then allow SSH from the bastion to application hosts in private subnets. Route tables direct which traffic leaves via the Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, or VPC Endpoint. Misconception: adding a NAT Gateway to a private subnet does not make it publicly reachable; NAT allows outbound connections while preventing inbound initiations. Key takeaway: ensure route tables align with your security posture — private subnets should never have their default route pointing to an Internet Gateway. Subnetting and Routing Strategy means public subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to igw; private subnets route outbound via nat or vpc endpoints and should not have igw default routes.. In practical terms, design public and private subnets and choose routing targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Routing rule
keyIdea.text: Public subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW; private subnets route outbound via NAT or VPC Endpoints and should not have IGW default routes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Subnetting & Routing
Step-by-step

Designing subnets and routes

1. Define CIDR blocks
Choose ranges that accommodate growth and segmentation, e.g., 10.0.1.0/24 for public, 10.0.2.0/24 for private.
2. Attach Internet Gateway to public subnets
Set route table entries for 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW for public subnets.
3. Private subnets use NAT or Endpoints
Use NAT for general outbound internet; use VPC Endpoints to reach AWS services privately.
Concrete example
Public Subnet CIDR: 10.0.1.0/24 — route 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-12345 Private Subnet CIDR: 10.0.2.0/24 — route 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-67890 or route s3 via vpce-abcde
Misconception check
Giving a private subnet a default route to a NAT Gateway does not make it internet-reachable from the outside; NAT supports outbound-only initiation.
Key Takeaway

Map routes to intent: IGW for public ingress, NAT for controlled outbound, and endpoints for private service access.

screens.title: Route Tables and Gateway Endpoint Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: A Gateway Endpoint for S3 integrates into a subnet's route table as a target so traffic to S3 prefix lists is routed internally. Conceptually, you create the endpoint, select the VPC and the route tables for private subnets, and the console adds routes like destination "pl-63a5400a" mapped to the endpoint. To verify, inspect the private subnet's route table and confirm there is an entry for the S3 prefix list pointing to the endpoint target. A concrete test is to launch an EC2 instance in the private subnet with a Security Group that allows outbound HTTPS and then run a simple AWS CLI command such as aws s3 ls from the instance using a bastion hop to reach it. If the endpoint is configured correctly, the S3 call succeeds even though the subnet has no Internet Gateway or NAT. Misconception: creating an endpoint does not bypass IAM or bucket policies; you must still ensure the instance's role and resource policies permit the action. Key takeaway: route table verification plus an in-subnet S3 test proves the endpoint operates as intended. Route Tables and Gateway Endpoint Configuration means confirm the route table contains the s3 prefix list route to the endpoint and validate by running aws s3 ls from a private instance with appropriate role permissions.. In practical terms, how a gateway endpoint appears in a route table and how to verify it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Gateway Endpoint & Route Table
What you configure

Create Gateway Endpoint and associate route tables

Select service: S3 (Gateway). Choose your VPC and pick the route tables used by private subnets. The route table receives an entry pointing S3 prefix list to the endpoint target.
Verification steps
  1. Confirm a new route exists for the S3 prefix list pointing to the endpoint.
  2. Launch an EC2 in the private subnet with outbound HTTPS allowed.
  3. From the instance, run a test like aws s3 ls to ensure access without IGW or NAT.
Command example
# From a private instance with proper IAM role:
aws s3 ls

# Expected: list of buckets if endpoint and permissions are correct
If the command fails, check the route table for the S3 prefix list entry, the endpoint association, and the instance's IAM role and Security Group egress rules.
Key Takeaway

A Gateway Endpoint adds a route table target for S3; verify with route table inspection and an in-subnet S3 API call.

screens.title: Internet Gateway and NAT Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: An Internet Gateway enables resources in a subnet to send and receive traffic to and from the internet when a route table directs 0.0.0.0/0 to that gateway. Use this only for subnets that must be reachable from the internet, such as load balancers or public-facing services. A NAT Gateway provides outbound internet access for instances in private subnets while preventing the internet from initiating connections to them. For example, place a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and configure the private subnet's route table to direct outbound 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT. This pattern allows instances to download OS updates or call external APIs without exposing their private IPs. Misconception: a NAT Gateway does not allow inbound connections to private instances; it only translates outbound traffic for return. Consider cost and availability when using NAT Gateways: they are charged for hourly and data transfer usage. When cost or privacy is the primary concern for AWS service access, prefer VPC Endpoints where supported. Key takeaway: use IGW for public ingress, NAT for controlled outbound needs, and endpoints for private AWS service access to reduce exposure and cost.

keyIdea.text: IGW provides inbound/outbound internet for public subnets; NAT Gateway allows outbound-only internet for private subnets while preventing inbound initiation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Internet & NAT Gateways
Internet Gateway (IGW)

Public ingress and egress

Attach to your VPC and add a route for 0.0.0.0/0 in public subnet route tables. Use for load balancers and public services.

Example
Public web servers receive traffic through IGW routes and public IP addresses.
NAT Gateway

Outbound-only internet access

Deployed in public subnets; private subnet route tables send outbound traffic to NAT so instances can access the internet without public IPs.

Operational note
NAT incurs hourly and data costs. Use VPC Endpoints for AWS service access where possible to avoid NAT charges and reduce exposure.
Key Takeaway

Choose IGW only for public-facing subnets and use NAT or endpoints for private subnet outbound needs to maintain isolation.

screens.title: DNS Resolution and Route 53 Resolver Endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: VPCs use an AWS-provided DNS resolver by default for name resolution inside the network. For enhanced control or integration with on-premises DNS, use Route 53 Resolver Endpoints. These endpoints allow two-way DNS forwarding between your VPC and on-premises systems, enabling centralized name resolution and application of DNS-based security policies. A practical example: forward internal domain queries from your VPC to an on-premises resolver for legacy hostnames, while letting AWS resolve service endpoints by default. Misconception: changing DNS settings does not alter network routing or firewall rules; it only affects how names are resolved to IPs. Always ensure that DNS changes are coordinated with network policies. Key takeaway: use Route 53 Resolver Endpoints when you need DNS integration across environments or central control for DNS filtering, and continue to audit resolution paths as part of your security posture. DNS Resolution and Route 53 Resolver Endpoints means use route 53 resolver endpoints to forward and centralize dns resolution between vpcs and on-premises, enabling unified policies and filtering.. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › DNS & Route 53 Resolver
Default behavior

VPC DNS resolver

AWS provides a default resolver for name lookups. Use it for typical service discovery and internal DNS names.

When to add Route 53 Resolver
If you need two-way DNS forwarding to on-premises or centralized DNS filtering, create Resolver Endpoints to forward queries.
Concrete example
Forward internal queries for legacy.example.local from the VPC to your on-premises DNS via a Route 53 Resolver endpoint so applications can resolve legacy hostnames.
Operational note
DNS changes require coordination with routing and firewall rules — resolution alone won't open traffic paths.
Key Takeaway

Use Route 53 Resolver Endpoints to centralize DNS policies and enable two-way resolution with on-premises networks while keeping network controls intact.

screens.title: Secure a Private Subnet: NACLs and S3 Gateway Endpoint
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity follows the chapter scenario: you have a VPC with a public and private subnet. The goal is to secure the private subnet with a strict NACL and enable private S3 access via a Gateway Endpoint. First, create or confirm VPC subnets and CIDR blocks such as 10.0.1.0/24 for public and 10.0.2.0/24 for private. Next, create a NACL named PrivateSubnetNACL and associate it with the private subnet. Add inbound rules that permit only the minimal traffic you need — for example TCP 80 and 443 from the public subnet, TCP 22 from the bastion host’s subnet for administration, and allow internal subnet traffic. Remember to add outbound rules mirroring necessary return ranges including ephemeral 1024–65535, because NACLs are stateless. Then create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3, select the VPC, and associate the private subnet's route table so the console adds a route for the S3 prefix list pointing to the endpoint. Finally, launch a private EC2, ensure its Security Group allows outbound HTTPS, and from the private instance run aws s3 ls after connecting via a bastion host to confirm S3 access. Misconception: the NACL must allow ephemeral outbound ports for return traffic; without them, traffic will be blocked even though an inbound rule exists. Key takeaway: this pattern demonstrates how combining explicit subnet filters with private endpoints provides secure and private service access.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hands-on: Secure Private Subnet

Lab steps (summary)

  1. Confirm VPC and subnets: Public 10.0.1.0/24, Private 10.0.2.0/24.
  2. Create PrivateSubnetNACL and associate with the private subnet.
  3. Add inbound ALLOW rules for necessary traffic and outbound ALLOW rules including ephemeral ports 1024–65535.
  4. Create Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 and associate the private subnet's route table.
  5. Launch private EC2, ensure Security Group allows outbound 443, and test aws s3 ls via bastion hop.
Important note
NACLs are stateless; forgetting outbound ephemeral ports is the most common source of failures in this lab.
Command to validate
# From the private instance (after bastion hop)
aws s3 ls

# Expect: a list of buckets if endpoint and IAM policies are correct
Troubleshooting tips
  • Check the route table for the S3 prefix list route to the endpoint.
  • Verify NACL outbound ephemeral port allowances.
  • Confirm the instance role has S3 list permissions.
Key Takeaway

Combining strict NACLs with a Gateway Endpoint gives private, auditable access to S3 without exposing the subnet to the internet.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap three essential concepts. First, the VPC is an isolated virtual network where subnetting and route tables determine exposure — treat routes as policy decisions. Second, Security Groups are stateful, instance-level firewalls that only allow specified traffic and implicitly deny everything else; use them for least-privilege and inter-tier group references. Third, NACLs act at the subnet level, are stateless, and support explicit DENY rules evaluated in numeric order; use NACLs for subnet-wide protections but change them cautiously. Each of these ideas helps you decide where to place protections and how to verify them. As you design, always combine these controls to create layered defenses: routes decide where traffic can go, NACLs can block bad actors at the edge, and Security Groups protect individual resources. Ask yourself: which control best enforces the requirement — a per-instance rule, a subnet deny, or a private service endpoint?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of an AWS Virtual Private Cloud and the controls that keep its perimeter and internal segments secure. We will treat the VPC like a virtual data center: there are instance-level firewalls called Security Groups, subnet-level filters called Network Access Control Lists, routing choices that determine which resources see the internet, and VPC Endpoints that let services talk privately inside the AWS backbone. You will see concrete examples such as allowing SSH only from a trusted IP range, how NACL rules are ordered and stateless, and how a Gateway Endpoint lets a private EC2 instance call S3 without an internet path. I will also point out common mistakes, like opening port 22 to the world or misordering NACL deny rules, and explain why auditing and DNS configuration matter as ongoing tasks. By the end of this chapter you will understand the relationships between these controls and be able to choose the right pattern to isolate sensitive resources while allowing necessary service access. Keep in mind: security in a VPC is layered and continuous, not a one-time checkbox.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use to secure a VPC. First, you will be able to identify and describe core VPC components and how they interrelate, so you can reason about where to place protection. Second, you will learn to configure Security Groups correctly for least-privilege access, including concrete examples like permitting SSH only from a trusted management IP. Third, you will gain the ability to design and apply Network ACLs at the subnet level, and understand how stateless rules require explicit return port allowances. Fourth, you will learn how to choose and configure VPC Endpoints so service traffic stays on the AWS network and avoids the public internet. Each objective includes a competency milestone you can verify: describe the control, configure a minimal rule set, and validate behavior with a simple connection test.

These objectives extend to operational skills and verification steps you will practice. First, you will configure subnetting and route tables to separate public and private resources, and justify why default routes to an Internet Gateway must not exist for private subnets. Second, you will be able to plan NAT Gateway use cases versus VPC Endpoints, knowing when to accept NAT costs and when a Gateway Endpoint is a better privacy choice. Third, you will configure DNS resolution and, when necessary, Route 53 Resolver endpoints to integrate with on-premises systems while retaining central control. Fourth, you will perform audit and remediation checks using automated tools and manual validation techniques to detect misconfigurations such as overly permissive Security Group rules or improper NACL orders. Each objective includes a verification step so you can test the expected behavior in a lab environment.

A Virtual Private Cloud, or VPC, is a logically isolated portion of the AWS network where you create subnets, route tables, and gateways to control traffic. Think of it as your cloud data center. You define IP ranges with CIDR blocks and decide which subnets are public or private based on where you place an Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, or VPC Endpoints. A concrete example: you might create a VPC with two subnets — a public subnet for a load balancer attached to an Internet Gateway and a private subnet for application servers that never receive incoming internet traffic. That private subnet can still reach S3 privately through a Gateway Endpoint, avoiding the internet entirely. A common misconception is that resources inside a VPC are automatically private; in fact, a subnet becomes public when its route table directs 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway. So you must design subnets and routes deliberately. Key takeaway: the VPC is the foundation for all subsequent network controls. When you design one, draw expected traffic paths and explicitly map which control (Security Group, NACL, route table, endpoint) enforces each boundary.

Security Groups are the primary instance-level firewall in AWS. They are stateful, which means once you permit an outbound request, the return traffic is implicitly allowed even if there is no explicit inbound rule for that return path. You attach one or more Security Groups to an EC2 instance or other supported resource and define only what is allowed; everything else is implicitly denied. A practical example: to allow SSH administration, add an inbound rule for TCP port 22 from your management IP range only. Avoid the common mistake of opening port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0, which exposes your hosts to the world. Security Groups support referencing other security groups as sources, which is a powerful pattern for allowing traffic from a specific application tier without relying on IPs. Misconception check: because Security Groups are permissive-only, you cannot explicitly deny traffic at the Security Group level. If you need explicit deny semantics, that is where NACLs can complement Security Groups at the subnet boundary. Key takeaway: design Security Groups for least privilege, reuse group references for tiers, and keep administration ports limited to known addresses.

Network Access Control Lists operate at the subnet boundary and are stateless. That means every direction of traffic must be explicitly allowed: if you allow inbound TCP 80, you must also allow outbound ephemeral ports such as 1024–65535 to permit return traffic. NACLs support both ALLOW and DENY rules and rules are evaluated in order by rule number from lowest to highest. When a packet matches a rule, that rule immediately applies and no further rules are processed. This ordered processing is a critical operational detail. A common use case is to place a NACL on a private subnet to block known malicious IP ranges before traffic reaches instances. But be cautious: adding DENY rules can inadvertently block legitimate traffic if rule numbers or ranges are not precise. Always test NACL changes in non-production or during a maintenance window. Concrete example: a NACL with a low-numbered DENY for a malicious IP will stop that IP at the subnet edge even if an instance Security Group would otherwise allow it. Key takeaway: NACLs are powerful gatekeepers but require careful ordering and explicit return rules because they are stateless.

Understanding the difference between Security Groups and NACLs is crucial for proper VPC design. Security Groups are stateful and apply to instances; they are permissive-only and ideal for defining which ports or sources an application tier accepts. NACLs are stateless, apply to subnets, and can include explicit deny rules. A practical contrast: if you want to prevent all traffic from a known malicious IP to an entire subnet, a low-numbered DENY in a NACL will stop that traffic before it reaches instances. Conversely, to restrict SSH to a particular management host for a single server, a Security Group rule referencing the management host's IP is cleaner and easier to manage. Another important operational note is order: NACLs process rules by number and stop at a match; Security Groups evaluate all rules together. Misconception: Security Groups cannot block traffic explicitly; they only allow. Use them for least-privilege access and use NACLs sparingly for broader deny patterns. The key takeaway: combine both controls — Security Groups for per-resource permissions, NACLs for subnet-level policies — and test changes because their behaviors differ in statefulness and rule processing.

VPC Endpoints let resources talk to supported AWS services privately over the AWS network. There are two primary types you need to know: Gateway Endpoints and Interface Endpoints. Gateway Endpoints apply to S3 and DynamoDB. They are configured as a target in a route table and are free to use. An example: add a Gateway Endpoint for S3 to the private subnet's route table; EC2 instances can then upload to S3 without a NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway. Interface Endpoints use AWS PrivateLink and create an elastic network interface with a private IP in your subnet. They support many services and partner endpoints, but they incur charges. Use Interface Endpoints when Gateway Endpoints are not supported or when you need finer-grained control. A practical design: prefer Gateway Endpoints for S3 traffic to avoid NAT costs and reduce attack surface; use Interface Endpoints when you need private access to other AWS services. Misconception: endpoints always eliminate the need for secure policies — you still must use IAM and bucket policies to enforce access control. Key takeaway: choose the endpoint type by service and cost trade-off and associate endpoints with the correct route tables or subnets.

A secure subnetting and routing strategy separates internet-facing components from private resources. Start by defining CIDR blocks and dividing them into public and private subnets. Public subnets should have a route to an Internet Gateway for workloads that need inbound access, like public load balancers. Private subnets should not have a default route to an Internet Gateway. Instead, private subnets often send outbound traffic through a NAT Gateway when instances need to reach the internet for updates, or through VPC Endpoints to reach AWS services privately. A typical design: place bastion hosts in a public subnet that only accepts SSH from an operations IP, then allow SSH from the bastion to application hosts in private subnets. Route tables direct which traffic leaves via the Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, or VPC Endpoint. Misconception: adding a NAT Gateway to a private subnet does not make it publicly reachable; NAT allows outbound connections while preventing inbound initiations. Key takeaway: ensure route tables align with your security posture — private subnets should never have their default route pointing to an Internet Gateway. Subnetting and Routing Strategy means public subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to igw; private subnets route outbound via nat or vpc endpoints and should not have igw default routes.. In practical terms, design public and private subnets and choose routing targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For example, place a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and configure the private subnet's route table to direct outbound 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT. This pattern allows instances to download OS updates or call external APIs without exposing their private IPs. Misconception: a NAT Gateway does not allow inbound connections to private instances; it only translates outbound traffic for return. Consider cost and availability when using NAT Gateways: they are charged for hourly and data transfer usage. When cost or privacy is the primary concern for AWS service access, prefer VPC Endpoints where supported. Key takeaway: use IGW for public ingress, NAT for controlled outbound needs, and endpoints for private AWS service access to reduce exposure and cost.

VPCs use an AWS-provided DNS resolver by default for name resolution inside the network. For enhanced control or integration with on-premises DNS, use Route 53 Resolver Endpoints. These endpoints allow two-way DNS forwarding between your VPC and on-premises systems, enabling centralized name resolution and application of DNS-based security policies. A practical example: forward internal domain queries from your VPC to an on-premises resolver for legacy hostnames, while letting AWS resolve service endpoints by default. Misconception: changing DNS settings does not alter network routing or firewall rules; it only affects how names are resolved to IPs. Always ensure that DNS changes are coordinated with network policies. Key takeaway: use Route 53 Resolver Endpoints when you need DNS integration across environments or central control for DNS filtering, and continue to audit resolution paths as part of your security posture. DNS Resolution and Route 53 Resolver Endpoints means use route 53 resolver endpoints to forward and centralize dns resolution between vpcs and on-premises, enabling unified policies and filtering.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This hands-on activity follows the chapter scenario: you have a VPC with a public and private subnet. The goal is to secure the private subnet with a strict NACL and enable private S3 access via a Gateway Endpoint. First, create or confirm VPC subnets and CIDR blocks such as 10.0.1.0/24 for public and 10.0.2.0/24 for private. Next, create a NACL named PrivateSubnetNACL and associate it with the private subnet. Add inbound rules that permit only the minimal traffic you need — for example TCP 80 and 443 from the public subnet, TCP 22 from the bastion host’s subnet for administration, and allow internal subnet traffic. Remember to add outbound rules mirroring necessary return ranges including ephemeral 1024–65535, because NACLs are stateless. Then create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3, select the VPC, and associate the private subnet's route table so the console adds a route for the S3 prefix list pointing to the endpoint. Finally, launch a private EC2, ensure its Security Group allows outbound HTTPS, and from the private instance run aws s3 ls after connecting via a bastion host to confirm S3 access. Misconception: the NACL must allow ephemeral outbound ports for return traffic; without them, traffic will be blocked even though an inbound rule exists. Key takeaway: this pattern demonstrates how combining explicit subnet filters with private endpoints provides secure and private service access.

Let's recap three essential concepts. First, the VPC is an isolated virtual network where subnetting and route tables determine exposure — treat routes as policy decisions. Second, Security Groups are stateful, instance-level firewalls that only allow specified traffic and implicitly deny everything else; use them for least-privilege and inter-tier group references. Third, NACLs act at the subnet level, are stateless, and support explicit DENY rules evaluated in numeric order; use NACLs for subnet-wide protections but change them cautiously. Each of these ideas helps you decide where to place protections and how to verify them. As you design, always combine these controls to create layered defenses: routes decide where traffic can go, NACLs can block bad actors at the edge, and Security Groups protect individual resources. Ask yourself: which control best enforces the requirement — a per-instance rule, a subnet deny, or a private service endpoint?

Here are three final reminders to carry forward. First, use Gateway VPC Endpoints for S3 when possible so private instances can access S3 without a NAT or Internet Gateway, reducing attack surface and cost. Second, always test NACL changes in non-production and check rule order because a single DENY at a low number can block intended traffic. Third, auditing and DNS control are ongoing responsibilities — run configuration checks and use Route 53 Resolver endpoints for controlled DNS forwarding when integrating with on-premises systems. Each of these points supports a secure operational posture: minimizing public exposure, preventing accidental blocks, and keeping name resolution predictable and auditable. Before you finish, reflect on which endpoint, routing, and filtering choices will reduce your risk while meeting application needs.
